interview_metadata.name: Angel Diaz
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) ??? Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Santa Ana, California, in 1966, to parents who came from Mexico before I was born. We spoke Spanish at home and English at school, and my parents were very strict about respect, church, work, and helping the family. I grew up with brothers and cousins around all the time, so the house was noisy, but there was always food on the stove and somebody stopping by. I went to public schools in Santa Ana and later took some classes at community college, mostly practical things, but I did not finish a degree because I needed to work. I got into painting young, first helping on small jobs and learning prep work, masking, sanding, matching colors, and how to leave a place clean. I married my husband Roberto in my twenties, and we raised two children, Marisol and Daniel. The biggest parts of my life have been family, steady work, church, and staying connected to my Mexican roots while building a life here in Orange County. Now I live in Seal Beach, still work as a painter, swim and walk early in the morning, cook for my family, and I am thinking seriously about turning my experience into a small family painting business.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember most clearly from childhood?
follow_ups.response: Saturday mornings. My mother would have music on, usually rancheras, and we would clean before anyone was allowed to go play. Then later there might be tamales, cousins, or a church event.

follow_ups.question: When did painting become more than just a job?
follow_ups.response: Probably in my thirties, when customers started asking for me by name. I realized I had an eye for color and detail, and younger workers came to me when something had to be done right.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, the big one was when my children were still small and I had to decide whether to stay doing part-time, lower-paid work or commit fully to painting as a trade. At that time a contractor I knew offered to train me more seriously, including blueprint reading and commercial jobs, but it meant longer days and proving myself on crews where most people were men. Roberto and I talked it through at the kitchen table because child care and money were tight. I decided to take it, and I had to learn fast: how to prep correctly, how to talk to clients, how to be assertive without making enemies. That choice gave me confidence and a skill I could carry for decades. It also shaped how I teach younger painters now, especially women or bilingual workers who may not always feel listened to.

follow_ups.question: What made you say yes even though it was difficult?
follow_ups.response: I wanted steady skills, not just whatever hours someone gave me. I also wanted my kids to see their mother could stand on her own feet.

follow_ups.question: Who supported you most during that transition?
follow_ups.response: Roberto helped with the kids, and an older painter named Manny taught me without talking down to me. My mother helped with meals when I worked late.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I remember deciding that if I was going to work that hard, I wanted to become truly skilled and respected, not just be somebody holding a brush.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel sure right away?
follow_ups.response: No, I was nervous, especially on commercial sites. But once I learned the routine, I felt proud.

follow_ups.question: How did that decision change your daily life?
follow_ups.response: My days became more structured. I packed lunches, planned child care, and started treating work like a long-term profession.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. Affordable child care and more formal training programs for women in trades would have helped. I learned mostly by proving myself on the job, which works, but it can be hard and lonely.

follow_ups.question: What kind of support would have made the biggest difference?
follow_ups.response: A paid apprenticeship with clear steps and someone to call when a crew was treating you unfairly.

follow_ups.question: Did any organization help later on?
follow_ups.response: Later, safety classes and OSHA trainings helped me become more confident and professional.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Roberto Diaz. We have been married more than thirty years, and he is steady, quiet, and very family-minded. We have two adult children. Marisol lives in Long Beach and works in a school office, and Daniel lives in Garden Grove and does electrical work. They are grown, but we still see each other often, usually Sunday dinner or birthdays, and I talk to Marisol almost every day. I also have grandchildren through Marisol, and they bring a lot of joy and noise into the house when they visit. Family is not just holidays for us; it is helping with rides, food, repairs, and checking on each other. Roberto and I are trying to plan for retirement, but I also want the kids involved if we start the small painting contractor business.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal family gathering look like?
follow_ups.response: Usually I cook carnitas, rice, beans, salsa, and maybe mole if I have time. People come around midafternoon, the kids run in and out, and somebody always puts music on.

follow_ups.question: Who do you rely on day to day?
follow_ups.response: Roberto first, then Marisol. My sister Teresa is also someone I call when I need honest advice.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a sister, Teresa, in Anaheim, and a younger brother, Luis, in Riverside. We are close, though everyone is busy, and we mostly connect by phone and family events.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see them?
follow_ups.response: Teresa maybe twice a month, Luis more like every couple months unless there is a birthday or holiday.

follow_ups.question: What role do they play in your life?
follow_ups.response: Teresa is the one I laugh with and complain to. Luis helps with practical things when he can.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes, I have good friends through church, swimming, walking, and my book club. My closest friend outside family is Carmen, who I met through church potlucks years ago. We swim together sometimes and trade recipes. I also have a walking group that meets early, and a few women from book club who know all my opinions about mystery novels. At work I have people I trust too, especially younger painters I have trained. Those relationships keep me from only thinking about work and family obligations.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Carmen?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week, either after Mass, at swimming, or when we cook for a church event.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your book club usually read?
follow_ups.response: A lot of mysteries. I like Agatha Christie for the puzzle and Gillian Flynn when I want something darker.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Seal Beach, not far from the coast. It is quieter than where I grew up, and I like that I can get to the beach early for a walk or swim. There are older residents, families, small restaurants, and people who know each other by sight even if they do not know names. It can be expensive, so you feel that pressure, but the weather and the ocean are a blessing. I like being close to Long Beach and the rest of Orange County because my family and jobs are spread around. There is also a mix of cultures, and I appreciate being able to find Mexican groceries, church events, and community activities nearby.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: The beach path, the grocery store, church, and the pool where the senior swim club meets.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few. We are friendly, and I have painted or touched up things for two neighbors over the years.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I am careful early in the morning, but Seal Beach feels calm compared with some busier places where I have worked.

follow_ups.question: What precautions do you take?
follow_ups.response: I walk with the group before sunrise, carry my phone, and avoid empty parking lots.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that worried you?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-ins or news about scams targeting older people, nothing violent close to me.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is the ocean, the quiet, and the community feel. The hard part is the cost, parking during busy weekends, and sometimes feeling like working families are being priced out.

follow_ups.question: What would make it better for you?
follow_ups.response: More affordable services and housing options for regular working people, not just people with big retirement savings.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: The routine, the beach, church nearby, and being close enough to our children.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me and my husband Roberto in the home. It is quieter than when the kids were young, but we still keep the house ready for family. Roberto handles a lot of repairs and errands, and I do most of the cooking and organizing, though we both share bills and decisions. The grandchildren visit, but they do not live with us. Sometimes a relative stays overnight after a family event, but no one else is part of the household.

follow_ups.question: What are your household routines together?
follow_ups.response: Coffee early, work or errands during the day, dinner around six or seven, and TV or phone calls with family at night.

follow_ups.question: Do you and Roberto divide chores pretty clearly?
follow_ups.response: Yes. He handles trash, repairs, and cars; I handle meals, laundry planning, and the calendar. We both clean.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just me and Roberto.

follow_ups.question: No one staying for work or school?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, the household has been stable.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Our grandchildren may sleep over some weekends, and sometimes my sister stays after a late family gathering.

follow_ups.question: How often do the grandchildren stay?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month.

follow_ups.question: Do you prepare differently when they come?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I buy fruit, cereal, and things they like, and I put away work supplies.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: No adult child away at school?
follow_ups.response: No, both children have their own homes.

follow_ups.question: No one hospitalized?
follow_ups.response: No, thank God.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: On workdays I wake around 5:15, have coffee, stretch my knees and shoulders, and either walk or swim if the job starts later. Painting work can start early, especially commercial jobs, so I pack lunch and leave by 6:30 or 7. Mondays and Tuesdays are usually heavier workdays, with prep, sanding, patching, and organizing materials. Wednesdays I sometimes have book club in the evening. Thursdays or Fridays might be church volunteering or checking on family. Weekends are for groceries, cooking, Mass, family meals, and sometimes community theater set painting or volunteer home repair projects.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 9:30 or 10, earlier if I have been on ladders all day.

follow_ups.question: Which day feels most social?
follow_ups.response: Sunday, because of Mass and family dinner.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a professional painter on residential and commercial projects. I do surface prep, patching, sanding, priming, color matching, brushing, rolling, sometimes spraying, and final walkthroughs with customers. I also help coordinate small crews, especially newer workers who need training on safety and clean work habits. My schedule depends on the project, but usually Monday through Friday, early morning to midafternoon or late afternoon. Sometimes there is weekend work if a business needs painting while closed. I am also preparing for more supervisory work and looking into lead-safe certification.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job takes the most skill?
follow_ups.response: Prep and color matching. People notice the final color, but if the wall is not prepared right, everything fails.

follow_ups.question: Do you work for one employer or different contractors?
follow_ups.response: Mostly with one painting contractor now, with some side referrals, but I am trying to keep things organized and legitimate.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the family calendar, help with church potlucks, tend my backyard herbs and chilies, and check in on my older aunt by phone. I also do the shopping because I am particular about produce and spices. On Tuesdays or Thursdays, depending on the week, I swim with the senior group. I read at night, usually mysteries. I also spend time looking at paint products and more eco-friendly materials because of the business idea.

follow_ups.question: What do you grow in the garden?
follow_ups.response: Cilantro, mint, oregano, tomatoes sometimes, and chilies when the weather is good.

follow_ups.question: How much time does church volunteering take?
follow_ups.response: Some weeks just an hour or two, but before a big potluck or festival it can take most of a Saturday.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I have been more intentional about swimming because my joints complain if I only work and do not stretch. I also cut back a little on saying yes to every volunteer request because I was overcommitting. Recently I started setting aside one evening a week to look into business classes and certification requirements. Work is still physical, but I am trying to shift toward supervising, estimating, and mentoring. That means my routine now includes more paperwork and planning than before.

follow_ups.question: What made you cut back on commitments?
follow_ups.response: I got exhausted before a church event and realized I was helping everyone except myself.

follow_ups.question: What business tasks are you learning?
follow_ups.response: Estimating labor, insurance basics, bookkeeping, and what licenses or certifications we would need.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are adults now, so I do not have school-year routines for them anymore. When they were young, mornings were rushed: breakfast, uniforms or school clothes, backpacks, and getting them to school before I went to work. After school they did homework at the kitchen table, church youth activities sometimes, and sports or music depending on the year. Now the school routines I hear about are for my grandchildren, and Marisol manages most of that.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with the grandchildren's routines?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I pick them up or watch them if Marisol has a late meeting.

follow_ups.question: What activities do they do?
follow_ups.response: One likes soccer, and the younger one likes art projects, especially painting with me.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally, I have not had serious trouble with law enforcement. I have been pulled over for small things, like a taillight, and I have called police once when there was suspicious activity near a job site. My feelings are mixed because I know officers can be helpful, but I also know Latino workers can be treated with suspicion, especially when driving work trucks or working in wealthier neighborhoods. I tell younger workers to keep their paperwork, insurance, and licenses in order because I do not want a small interaction becoming a big problem.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt profiled?
follow_ups.response: A couple of times, yes, mostly on job sites where people questioned whether we belonged there.

follow_ups.question: How do you talk about this with family?
follow_ups.response: We talk about being respectful but also knowing your rights and not assuming every situation is fair.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The Seal Beach police response to community issues stands out as generally calm, but I also remember seeing friends' sons stopped more often when they were young. That stays with you.

follow_ups.question: Were those friends close to you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, church families and neighbors from when the kids were growing up.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you raised your children?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with Daniel. We taught him to be careful during traffic stops.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and neither has Roberto or our children. I have had extended family members with DUI trouble years ago, but not in my immediate household.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your family?
follow_ups.response: It caused worry and embarrassment, but people handled it and moved forward.

follow_ups.question: Has it shaped how you view alcohol?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I am careful about driving after any drinking, and I tell the younger ones the same.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, especially in presidential elections and local elections when I understand the issues. I was taught that if you have a voice, you should use it, because my parents did not always feel they had that power when they first came here. I read the voter guide, ask my children about confusing propositions, and usually mail my ballot early. I do miss smaller special elections sometimes if I am overloaded with work, but I try not to.

follow_ups.question: What issues usually motivate you to vote?
follow_ups.response: Health care, schools, workers' rights, immigration, housing costs, and environmental safety.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but not all day. Roberto is quieter, and my children have strong opinions.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am moderate to liberal, and I usually lean Democratic. I care about working people, health care access, fair wages, immigration with dignity, and good public schools. At the same time, I believe in personal responsibility, family, faith, and not wasting money, so I do not like politics that feels like just shouting. My views come from lived experience: I have worked with my hands for decades, seen families struggle with rent and medical bills, and watched immigrant parents try to do everything right. I also care about safety and order, but I do not think safety should mean treating some communities as suspects. On environmental issues, I am practical; in painting, I have seen how chemicals and dust affect workers, so I support safer products and lead-safe rules. I am not a person who puts signs all over my yard, but I pay attention.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify strongly with a party?
follow_ups.response: I identify more with Democrats, but I do not like following any party blindly.

follow_ups.question: What would make you distrust a politician?
follow_ups.response: If they talk down to workers, use immigrants as a problem to blame, or promise things without explaining how to pay for them.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on housing and health care as I get older. When I was younger, I thought if you worked hard enough, you could manage, and I still believe work matters. But now I see people working full time and still not able to afford rent, medicine, or child care. I have also become more aware of environmental rules in the trades, especially lead paint and safer materials. I do not think my values changed completely; I just see more clearly how systems can make things harder for regular families.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic affect your views?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it showed how vulnerable workers are when they cannot work from home.

follow_ups.question: Have your children influenced you politically?
follow_ups.response: They have, especially on climate and racial justice. They push me to read more.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot. I am not Black, so I do not pretend it is my same experience, but as a Latina I understand being looked at differently. The videos and stories were painful, and they made me think about what families have to teach their sons just to stay safe. I also thought about workers of color on job sites and how quickly people assume something. It made conversations in my family more serious, especially with Daniel and my grandchildren growing up in a mixed community.

follow_ups.question: What part affected you most?
follow_ups.response: Seeing mothers talk about being afraid for their children. That is something I felt in my chest.

follow_ups.question: Did it change any behavior?
follow_ups.response: It made me speak more openly with family and church friends, instead of avoiding the subject.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the movement raises real issues about fairness, policing, and whose pain gets believed. I also think the conversation gets simplified on television, like you are either against police or against justice, and I do not see it that way. Communities need safety, but safety has to include accountability. I have thought a lot about training, mental health calls, and how quickly force is used. For me, faith also says every person has dignity, so ignoring racism is not acceptable.

follow_ups.question: Do people at church agree with you?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some are uncomfortable. The older generation sometimes wants to avoid conflict.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Better accountability, body cameras, less aggressive stops, and more services for mental health and homelessness.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is part of daily life whether people admit it or not. In my family, we benefited from opportunity here, but we also dealt with accents being judged, names being mispronounced, and assumptions about what kind of work we should do. I see younger people talking about identity more directly, and sometimes I learn from them. I also worry that people get defensive too quickly and stop listening. Race in the U.S. is complicated because it is history, money, schools, neighborhoods, and policing all together.

follow_ups.question: How do you describe your own identity?
follow_ups.response: Mexican American, Latina, Catholic, working woman, and Californian.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about race with your grandchildren?
follow_ups.response: In simple ways, yes. I tell them to be proud of who they are and respectful of others.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family, church friends, and coworkers. I did not join big protests, but I donated a small amount once and attended a local discussion at church about racism and faith.

follow_ups.question: Why not protest?
follow_ups.response: Partly work schedule, partly COVID concerns at the time, and partly I am more comfortable in smaller community settings.

follow_ups.question: What did you say in those conversations?
follow_ups.response: That listening is not the same as blaming yourself, and that accountability should matter to everyone.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My children are more outspoken than I am. Marisol posts articles and talks about school equity, and Daniel talks about how young men of color get treated. Roberto listens but does not like arguments, so he keeps it shorter. My church friends are mixed; some are very supportive, some think the topic is too political. In book club, we have discussed novels and documentaries that touch on race, and those conversations can be thoughtful.

follow_ups.question: Have any relationships become strained over it?
follow_ups.response: A little with acquaintances, not close family. I choose my words carefully.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: My children and some younger coworkers. They ask direct questions.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is decent for 59, but I have to take care of my joints and back because painting is physical. My knees and shoulders get stiff, especially after ladders, sanding, or overhead work. I swim and walk because low-impact exercise helps. I watch my blood pressure and try to eat balanced, though I love rich Mexican food and have to be sensible with portions. I do regular checkups and try not to ignore pain the way I did when I was younger.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any diagnosed chronic condition?
follow_ups.response: I have high blood pressure that is monitored, and mild arthritis-type joint pain, especially knees and hands.

follow_ups.question: What helps most day to day?
follow_ups.response: Swimming, stretching, good shoes, taking breaks, and not carrying everything myself.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: The easy part is living near places to walk and swim, and having friends who expect me to show up. The hard part is work fatigue, family meals with delicious food, and my habit of saying yes to too much. When I am busy, I may skip stretching or eat late. Health takes planning, the same as a painting job.

follow_ups.question: What foods do you try to limit?
follow_ups.response: Fried foods, too much pork, pan dulce, and salty snacks.

follow_ups.question: Who keeps you accountable?
follow_ups.response: Carmen from swimming and my daughter Marisol.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The biggest thing was shoulder pain from overhead painting last year. It was not a broken bone, but it scared me because I need my body for work. I went to the doctor, did some physical therapy exercises, and changed how I schedule overhead tasks. My blood pressure also needed closer watching, so I got more serious about walking and cutting salt. Nothing dramatic like surgery, but enough to remind me I am not thirty anymore.

follow_ups.question: Did the shoulder pain affect work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I had to ask younger crew members to take more overhead rolling for a while.

follow_ups.question: Are you still doing physical therapy?
follow_ups.response: Not formal visits now, but I still do the exercises at home.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has slowed me down but has not stopped me. I have learned to pace myself, use better equipment, and delegate heavy or repetitive tasks when I can.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work because of it?
follow_ups.response: A few days for the shoulder and once for a bad back flare, but not long periods.

follow_ups.question: Does it affect family care?
follow_ups.response: Only that I cannot lift the grandchildren like when they were smaller.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes. Roberto has had cholesterol and back issues, and my mother had diabetes before she passed. Those experiences made me more serious about food and checkups. I also check on my aunt because she is older and sometimes confused about appointments. In Latino families, health care often becomes a family project: someone drives, someone translates, someone cooks differently. It can be tiring, but that is what we do.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever translate medical information?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for older relatives who prefer Spanish.

follow_ups.question: Who helped when your mother was sick?
follow_ups.response: My sister Teresa and I did a lot of appointments and meals.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have usually managed, but it can be expensive and confusing. Insurance through work has not always been strong, especially in smaller contractor jobs. I have delayed dental work before because the cost was high, and Roberto delayed a specialist visit once until we were sure what insurance would cover. For basic care we do okay, but you have to make calls, compare bills, and be persistent. I am grateful we have not had to skip lifesaving care, but we have postponed things.

follow_ups.question: What care is hardest to afford?
follow_ups.response: Dental, vision, and physical therapy visits.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel respected by providers?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, especially when providers speak clearly and do not rush.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, mostly home remedies, not instead of doctors but alongside regular care. We use teas like manzanilla, ginger, and cinnamon, vapor rub, caldo when someone is sick, and arnica cream for soreness. My mother believed in certain traditional remedies, and some of them are comforting. I am careful, though, because blood pressure medicine and real medical issues need a doctor. I see it as family care, not magic.

follow_ups.question: What remedy do you use most?
follow_ups.response: Chamomile tea at night and arnica for sore muscles.

follow_ups.question: Do you tell your doctor?
follow_ups.response: If it is something I take regularly, yes, especially with blood pressure.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, maybe a glass of wine or a margarita at a family party, but not as a way to cope every day. When I am stressed, I cook, pray, swim, or clean something. I have seen alcohol cause trouble in families, so I am careful. If I am upset, I would rather call my sister or take a walk than drink too much.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, usually with food and family.

follow_ups.question: What is your first coping habit?

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?

follow_ups.question: Have you ever voted Republican?

follow_ups.question: How strong is your Democratic identity?

follow_ups.question: What frustrates you about Democrats?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes they promise too much or speak in a way that feels far from working people.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: When I was 16, I lived in Santa Ana, California.

follow_ups.question: What was your neighborhood like then?
follow_ups.response: Busy, mostly working families, lots of Spanish spoken, lots of kids.

follow_ups.question: Did you like it?

transcript.response: Yes, I lived with both my mother and father when I was 16.

follow_ups.question: Were they strict?

follow_ups.question: What did they emphasize?
follow_ups.response: Respect, work, faith, and helping family.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: I lived with my sister Teresa, my brother Luis, and for a while an older cousin stayed with us too.

follow_ups.question: Was the house crowded?

follow_ups.question: Did you share a room?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I shared with my sister.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: My father completed about sixth grade in Mexico.

follow_ups.question: Did he value education?
follow_ups.response: Very much, because he did not have much himself.

follow_ups.question: Could he read English?
follow_ups.response: Some, but Spanish was easier for him.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: My mother completed about elementary school, maybe fifth grade, in Mexico.

follow_ups.question: Did she read and write Spanish?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but her formal schooling was limited.

follow_ups.question: Did she help with homework?
follow_ups.response: She encouraged us, but English homework was harder for her.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my mother worked for pay while I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was it full time?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes full time, sometimes part time depending on family needs.

follow_ups.question: Did she also manage the home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she did both, which I appreciate more now.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked in laundry and housekeeping jobs. She cleaned rooms, washed linens, folded, organized supplies, and sometimes helped in kitchens for events. Her important duties were speed, cleanliness, and reliability. She came home tired but still cooked for us.

follow_ups.question: Where did she learn that work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly by doing it, from other women and supervisors.

follow_ups.question: Did she like the work?
follow_ups.response: She was proud of being reliable, but it was hard physical work.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for hotels and cleaning services in Orange County. Those businesses provided rooms, hospitality, cleaning, and laundry services. She was part of the behind-the-scenes work that guests rarely notice unless it is not done.

follow_ups.question: Was it close to home?
follow_ups.response: Usually a bus ride or carpool away.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: A few times, and I remember the smell of laundry soap.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my father worked for pay the whole time I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but my mother's income mattered too.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Very long hours, especially in busy seasons.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked in landscaping and maintenance. He planted, trimmed, repaired irrigation, hauled materials, and maintained apartment and commercial properties. His duties were physical labor, showing up early, solving problems, and keeping places looking cared for. He taught me that details matter.

follow_ups.question: Did his work influence your painting career?
follow_ups.response: Yes, he taught me pride in manual work and doing things cleanly.

follow_ups.question: Did he have his own business?
follow_ups.response: No, mostly worked for companies and property owners.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for landscaping companies and property maintenance businesses. They maintained apartment complexes, small commercial properties, yards, and outdoor areas. They did not make a product exactly; they provided upkeep, repairs, and landscaping services.

follow_ups.question: Was it steady work?
follow_ups.response: Mostly steady, but weather and contracts affected it.

follow_ups.question: Did he know the property owners?
follow_ups.response: Some, yes. He was respected because he was dependable.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am working less physically and more as a supervisor, trainer, or owner of a small family painting contractor business. I want it to be honest, safe, bilingual, and focused on good craftsmanship and safer materials. I hope to finish lead-safe certification and take a short business class so I do not make avoidable mistakes. Personally, I want Roberto and me to stay healthy, keep our home, help our children without controlling them, and enjoy the grandchildren. I would love to travel more, maybe Oaxaca again and someday Barcelona to see Gaudí's buildings. I do not need a fancy life. I want peace, enough money, strong family, good health, and work that leaves something behind.

follow_ups.question: Who would be involved in the business?
follow_ups.response: Maybe Daniel for technical advice, Marisol for office organization if she wants, and younger painters I trust.

follow_ups.question: What would success look like?
follow_ups.response: A small crew with steady jobs, safe practices, happy customers, and no cutting corners.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, faith, dignity in work, and keeping my word. I value my culture: Spanish, food, music, Día de los Muertos, and the way we gather when someone needs help. I value health more now because without it everything becomes harder. I also value beauty in ordinary things, like a clean painted wall, a good pot of mole, flowers in the yard, or salsa music after dinner. Mostly, I want to be remembered as someone who worked hard, loved deeply, and helped where she could.

follow_ups.question: What do you want your grandchildren to learn from you?
follow_ups.response: Be proud of who you are, work honestly, and do not forget family.

follow_ups.question: What value guides your decisions most often?
follow_ups.response: Responsibility, but I am learning that responsibility also means taking care of myself.
